H1.text: Push a heavy cupboard. Nothing. Push harder. Still nothing. Then, all at once, it jerks forward.

H2.text: Why does it stay stuck, and then give way so suddenly?

H3.text: Diya pushes her grandmother's steel trunk, to sweep under it.

H4.text: Starting it takes all her strength. But once it slides, a gentler push keeps it going. Why?

H5.text: The answer is two kinds of friction. Static, and kinetic.

P2.text: When one surface tries to slide over another, the surface pushes back along the contact. That force is friction.

P3.text: If the body is still at rest, it is static friction. It opposes the sliding that is about to start.

P4.text: If the body is already sliding, it is kinetic friction. It opposes the sliding that is going on.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. Diya's trunk, forty kilograms. She pushes, slowly harder and harder.

S2.text: Forty newtons. The trunk stays put. So friction is forty newtons too, pointing back.

S3.text: Eighty newtons. Still at rest. Friction is eighty. It grows to match her push.

S4.text: One hundred and sixty newtons. That is the most static friction can give. And the trunk gives way.

S5.text: At once, friction drops to one hundred and twenty. For a moment the push beats it, and the trunk speeds up, as Diya eases off.

S6.text: Now her push is one hundred and twenty. Push and friction balance, so the trunk slides at a steady speed.

S7.text: On the graph, friction climbs at forty five degrees, as big as the push. It peaks at one sixty, then drops to a flat line.

S8.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, as it gives way.

S9.text: Static friction is at its limit. Then friction falls to one twenty, and the extra forty newtons speed the trunk up.

D1.text: Now the rule, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. At rest, the net force is zero. So f s equals P.

D3.text: Step two. f s cannot grow forever. It is at most f s max.

D4.text: Step three. When P goes past f s max, the body starts to slide.

D5.text: Step four. While sliding, f k is nearly constant, and smaller than f s max.

D6.text: Step five. Then a equals P minus f k, over m.

T1.text: Remember this. Static friction matches the push, up to a limit. Kinetic friction is smaller, and nearly constant.

R1.text: But why is starting harder? Link by link.

R2.text: Zoom right in. Even smooth surfaces have tiny bumps. They touch only at a few points.

R3.text: At rest, these points press together and stick, like tiny welds.

R4.text: To start sliding, all of them must break at once.

R5.text: Once sliding, the points get no time to stick firmly. So kinetic friction is smaller.

K1.text: Side by side. Static: push a cupboard with fifty newtons, and friction is fifty. Push with seventy, and it is seventy.

K2.text: Kinetic: a sliding trunk feels one hundred and twenty newtons, whether it slides slowly or fast.

K3.text: Now you try. A book lies on a level table. Nobody pushes it. How big is the friction on it? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Zero! Nothing tries to slide the book, so friction has nothing to oppose.

V1.text: One more case. The trunk slides at one point two metres per second. Then Diya lets go.

V2.text: Your turn. While it slows down, is the friction static, or kinetic? Pause and decide.

V3.text: Kinetic! It is still sliding. One hundred and twenty newtons act back until it stops. Then friction is zero.

W2.text: A twenty five kilogram box. Static friction can reach ninety newtons, and kinetic friction is seventy. Find the friction and acceleration for pushes of sixty, and one hundred newtons.

W3.text: Sixty is less than ninety. The box stays at rest, so friction is sixty. Acceleration, zero.

W4.text: One hundred beats ninety. The box slides, so friction is kinetic. Seventy newtons.

W5.text: Net force, thirty newtons. a equals thirty over twenty five. One point two metres per second squared.

X2.text: Many students say a resting box always feels its maximum friction. So a sixty newton push meets ninety.

X3.text: But then the box would move backwards! Static friction only matches the push, up to its limit.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In questions where the push changes, and you find the friction at each stage.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A ten kilogram block. Static friction can reach fifty newtons, and kinetic friction is forty. A push of ten t newtons starts at t equals zero. Find the friction at three seconds, and the acceleration at eight. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Thirty newtons, and four metres per second squared.

A2.text: At three seconds the push is thirty, below fifty. At rest, so friction is thirty.

A3.text: At five seconds the push reaches fifty, and the block slides.

A4.text: At eight seconds, eighty minus forty is forty newtons. Over ten kilograms, four metres per second squared.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is the trunk harder to start than to keep sliding?

Y3.text: Two. A box pushed with thirty newtons does not move. What is the friction?

Y4.text: Three. Why does the friction graph drop suddenly?

N1.text: Next time: put a second trunk on top, and friction grows. By how much? One number, called mu, tells us. The coefficient of friction.
